extracted.intended_audience: members of the British Association, scientific administrators, and policymakers concerned with national science funding and organisation
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations and criteria for how the British Association (and by extension state/policy bodies) should prioritise and fund scientific research and organise national scientific institutions. Includes definitional criteria to distinguish 'Public' science from private enterprise and procedural recommendations for grants and long-term observational programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public science should be characterised by specific features
rubrics_metrics.description: Public science should be characterised by three principal features—(1) Continuity ; (2) Probability of Expansion ; (3) Unremunerativeness to the individual cultivating it, combined with profit or advantage to the community generally ; (4) Costliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each individual research, properly Public, may not present all these three features in equal prominence, but with the great mass of questions which come before the Association there will be no difficulty, in most cases, in arranging each under the proper category. Cases of doubtful character must be classified according to the discretion of the Association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish national (public) projects from private ones when making grants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Association, in making their grants, shall discriminate more than they have hitherto done between objects which are national and those which are not national ; and that they should give the preference to the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author proposes that preference be given to national/public objects (text context and subsequent recommendations treat such projects as those requiring Government support). Examples cited as 'Public Science': Kew Observatory, Sewage, Rainfall, Map of the Moon, and the Tides. The indiscriminate funding of many objects by private bodies can obscure which matters are proper duties of the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association should annually forward list of national research needs to Government
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of national scientific researches requiring immediate attention should be forwarded yearly by the Association to the Government, with such advice as to the best mode of conducting them as may seem necessary ; and that previous to each annual meeting the Association should request the Government to state what had been done with respect to such researches, the result being published in their annual volume of Proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural requirement is proposed so Government is informed and held to account; the Association need not seek collision but should pursue this to create a permanent system and expedite full consideration of state's duty to science.

rubrics_metrics.name: State should maintain institutions for research separate from teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: The State is bound, in the interests of the community, to maintain institutions—such as laboratories and observatories— for scientific research, apart from teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such institutions cannot be left entirely to private enterprise if they are to be maintained in efficiency; they are listed alongside museums, surveys, and botanical gardens as public responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single Minister and a permanent paid Consultative Council for science
rubrics_metrics.description: All State scientific institutions and action of every kind should be subject to the direction of a single Minister of State ; and such Minister of State should have the assistance of a permanent, paid, Consultative Council composed of eminent men of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These two measures (a Minister and a Council) are presented as fundamental to a consistent administrative system for science and among the most important steps the Royal Commission is considering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid undifferentiated small expedients that postpone proper State provision
rubrics_metrics.description: The Association's indiscriminate application of private funds to many objects can help justify undue reliance on private enterprise and postpone the establishment of adequate State provision for national scientific needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues for a bolder reorganisation (a 'radical cure') rather than continued small local applications; accepts risk that some projects might suffer neglect if referred to Government but prefers systematic, long-term organisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of long-term observational staff for lunar studies
rubrics_metrics.description: For close, prolonged study of lunar regions (e.g., Plato) a staff should consist of not less than six devoted observers working with instruments of varying aperture, carefully recording all their observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal qualifications: a keen eye for delicate variations of tint and detection of minute spots of light, with readiness to refer them by estimation and alignment to localities. Observations should not accumulate but be forwarded at once to an experienced selenographer for arrangement and discussion. Recommended programme length: not less than three years—five would most probably afford the best results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational data treatment: use chronological ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of observations under intervals of the luni-solar day fails to bring out any regularity in certain lunar variations; it is only by treating the observations chronologically that the true sequence of changes can be detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Committee's analysis the chronology of observations allowed detection of a correlation with the sun's altitude and the construction of a representative normal curve; methodological implication: choose data-organization that reveals true temporal sequences rather than artificial phase-binning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific education curricula should secure liberal development and emphasise laboratory work
rubrics_metrics.description: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology curriculum secures a liberal mental development and general culture as well as more strictly technical education; prominence is given to laboratory work in Physics, Chemistry, Assaying, Blowpipe Analysis, Metallurgy, and Ore-dressing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Institute's scheme devotes space to laboratories and promotes practical laboratory education as a marked feature—recommended as model material for those interested in scientific education and establishment of colleges of science.
